name: James VI and I
role: King of Scotland (1567-1625) and of England and Ireland (1603-1625)
summary: James defended hereditary monarchy as God's appointment and held that subjects may never resist even a bad king, though a king in a settled realm should rule by its laws and answers to God alone. He backed bishops and royal control of the church, opposed Puritan and papal claims, sought a union of England and Scotland, and kept peace abroad. His moral views were strict: death for witchcraft, sodomy among unpardonable crimes, and wives subordinate to husbands.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Mixed: he urged officials to set yearly price lists for merchants' wares, yet also wanted foreign merchants admitted so that wares would be better and cheaper (Basilikon Doron, advice on the Burghs).

property-fundamental.rationale: Mixed over time. The Trew Law (1598) calls the king overlord of all land and says subjects hold from him. Later he said the Common Law decides 'meum and tuum', that he wanted subjects secure in their possessions (1607), and that he submitted his own interests to the law (1616). Basilikon Doron also says not to rob the rich for pity of the poor.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Called tobacco a vile, harmful custom and in 1604 raised the import duty on it sharply, but did not ban it; tobacco is the only drug he addressed.

strong-leader.rationale: Held that the king may issue ordinances without Parliament's advice, that no Parliament law takes effect without his sceptre, and that the king rules by his own judgement ('that is my craft'). He did not frame this as bypassing gridlock.

state-harmful.rationale: Argued that even a tyrannical king is better than no king, because with no king 'nothing is unlawful to none' and order collapses.

limit-guns.rationale: Told his son to enforce his laws against guns and pistols sharply and to treat those who carry them as brigands and cut-throats. The context was feuding in Scotland, not gun ownership in general.

decide-locally.rationale: Inferred: told his son to stop heritable sheriffdoms and regalities from staying in great men's hands and to move Scotland toward English practice; in 1607 asked for one law for the whole island ('vnus Rex, vnus Grex, vna Lex').

traditional-family.rationale: Advised that a husband should command and his wife obey, that marriage is for restraint of lust, children and companionship, and that the king should rule as father of his people. He did not state the 'foundation of society' claim in these terms.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Inferred: Basilikon Doron lists sodomy among the crimes a king must never pardon and defines marriage by procreation and a wife as helper; he never discussed same-sex marriage itself.

gradual-change.rationale: Said novelties are dangerous in a body politic as in a natural body (1609) and that anything long and maturely established is made worse by innovation (1616); on the union he advised bringing change on 'with time and at leisure'.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Advised his son to permit and allure foreign merchants and craftsmen to come, citing England's gains from strangers. He wanted them kept out of principal offices of state.

free-trade.rationale: Wanted foreign merchants admitted so that wares would be best and cheapest, and asked in 1607 for 'communitie of commerce' between England and Scotland. He also set prices and levied a high tobacco duty, so the evidence is partial.

experts-over-public.rationale: Told the Commons not to meddle with 'the maine points of Government; that is my craft', and told judges they interpret law and do not make it. He meant the king and his officers, not credentialed experts.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Wrote that monarchy 'resembling the Diuinitie, approacheth nearest to perfection' and defended hereditary kingship at length.

democracy-best.rationale: Called monarchy the best form of government, and described the 'Democraticke forme of gouernment' sought by some Scottish ministers as a danger to church and state.

direct-votes.rationale: Inferred: held that laws are made by the king and are only 'craved' by subjects in Parliament, so he gave no role to votes by citizens on laws.

right-to-secede.rationale: Inferred: argued in 1603 that the union of England and Scotland was made by God ('what God hath conjoined let no man separate') and that nobody should 'cut asunder' the island; he did not discuss regional secession as such.

natural-rulers.rationale: Held that kings rule by birth and God's appointment, and told his son that that virtue often follows noble blood, and that virtue and vice run in families like inherited illness.

political-violence-never.rationale: Points both ways: rebellion against and killing of kings is never lawful in his view (and he denounced the Gunpowder Plot), but he held that just wars and executions are lawful.

separate-church-state.rationale: Told his son the king is 'Custos vtriusque Tabulae' and 'not mere laicus' but of mixed ecclesiastical and civil estate, and to rule the church himself; he was head of the established church.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Said in 1616 that God's law governs all municipal law and that law with no dependence on it is unjust. Basilikon Doron's sonnet tells kings to make all their laws spring from God's law. But in 1609 he said the judicial law of Moses suited only one people and time and preferred the Common Law for England.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Held that the sword is given only to the magistrate and not to private persons, and told his son to end private feuds and noble armed followings and the heritable jurisdictions of great men. He did not discuss private companies.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Held that subjects owe obedience absolutely and had put 'priuiledges' out of their hands by accepting a king; he also spoke of a king's duty to protect his subjects' possessions under law.

direct-action.rationale: Inferred: held that subjects may answer even a wicked king only with 'sobbes and teares to God', never resistance; his own stated route to change was through king and Parliament.

taxation-theft.rationale: Said a subject's goods and bodies are due to the king for defence and that 'one of the branches of duetie which Subiects owe to their Soueraigne, is Supply' (1609), asking Parliament for subsidies.

harm-principle.rationale: Basilikon Doron lists incest, sodomy and witchcraft among crimes never to be forgiven, and he condemned fornication; none turn on harm to others.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Declared in 1603 he would never give the first occasion of a breach and his reign was marked by peace (Treaty of London 1604); he held that wars must rest on just quarrels.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Mixed: held that the king is overlord and his subjects his vassals, and imposed an oath of allegiance, but told his son to break the nobles' private followings and feuds.

universal-morality.rationale: Wrote that God has imprinted in men's minds by the light of nature the love of the moral virtues, as seen in the virtuous lives of the old Romans.

single-common-good.rationale: Said the weal of the commonwealth must be the king's chief law, that king and people's weals cannot be separated, and told his son that Parliament must not be used for private interests.

rule-by-example.rationale: Told his son to make his life 'a law-booke and a mirrour' to his people, and quoted Claudian that edicts bend men less than the ruler's life. He also insisted on strict execution of laws.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Made Scripture the sole rule of conscience and called conscience not grounded on Scripture 'an ignorant fantasie, or an arrogant vanitie'.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Told his son never to let his wife meddle in political government and to keep her to household rule; he spoke of this as advice, not as law.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Said the king must procure 'the weale of both soules and bodies' of his subjects and prevent all dangers 'by all other meanes possible', including church, morals, trade and prices.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Mixed: told judges to show no respect of persons and told his son to make nobles keep the laws 'as precisely as the meanest'; but he held that kings are gods who can 'cry vp or downe' subjects like pawns, and that ranks are fixed by birth.

restrict-conversion.rationale: In 1609 said the law should 'strike seueriest' on apostates who leave the established church for Rome; he treated old-style Catholics more leniently.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Inferred: told his son to keep the schools, 'the seminarie of the Church', maintained so that doctrine is preserved in purity.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Held that kings hold power from God, not from the people, and that people who choose a king renounce the right to take power back.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Told his son to punish Puritans who refuse to obey the law and stir up rebellion and not to let their leaders stay in the land; he also forbade church meetings without his leave.

separated-powers.rationale: Said the king may not be controlled by Parliament, judges or people, that judges 'borrow' power from kings, and that it is sedition to dispute what a king may do.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Mixed: told his son to take up the quarrel of the poor against oppressors, but also to give judgement without favour to rich or poor and not rob the rich out of pity.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Said the king may suspend general laws for causes known to him (1598) and that the Gunpowder plot called for 'extraordinary Iudgement' (1605). Neither passage speaks of internal emergencies in general.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Advised his son to set a fixed price each year for the wares sold by merchants, and to let foreigners sell if merchants would not meet it; this is not limited to food or to scarcity.

party-controls-media.rationale: Told his son to prosecute keepers of seditious books (naming Buchanan and Knox) and to stop preachers meddling with state in the pulpit; this is censorship of sedition, not control of all media.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: No stated position on pooling sovereignty in a supranational union; uniting the English and Scottish crowns under one king is something nearby.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Held that the king appoints officers of state, makes war and peace, and disposes of offices without Parliament's assent; told his son to command armies in person.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Called parity of ministers 'mother of confusion', told his son to keep bishops and re-establish the three estates in Parliament, and McIlwain notes his later position 'no bishop, no king'.

clerical-rule.rationale: Told his son to chain bishops 'with such bondes' and denied that clergy or the Pope may rule kings.

recall-officials.rationale: Argued that a borough's people cannot displace their provost before election time, nor a flock its pastor, nor pupils a schoolmaster, so subjects may not remove a king.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Called Indians 'barbarous' and 'beastly' and Highlanders and islanders 'barbarous' and 'alluterly barbares', so he did rank cultures.

death-penalty.rationale: Wrote in Daemonologie that witches must be put to death, and in 1605 asked for 'Seueritie of punishment' for the Gunpowder plotters.

religious-exemptions.rationale: At Hampton Court in 1604 he rejected most Puritan requests for change, and in 1609 insisted that Catholic recusants be presented under the law.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Same position: kings succeed by birthright and no election gives or withdraws their power.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Said subjects' goods and bodies are due to the king for defence, though only through the settled laws of the realm.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Told his son to rule the church, keep church meetings under his permission, chain the bishops and annul the Act of Annexation; denied that the Pope may depose a king.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Told his son to be 'communis parens' to all, belonging to no surname or kin; in 1603 spoke of himself as the head uniting the two kingdoms.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Wanted 'a perfect Vnion of Lawes and persons' in 1607 and 'one Law' for the island, saying Scotland's laws should conform to England's (1616), while also saying Scotland should keep some particular privileges.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Wrote that kings are 'iustly called Gods', sit on God's throne, and are 'anointed of the Lord'; he did not claim divine descent.

character-from-environment.rationale: Wrote that education helps nature, but what is 'bred in the bone' is hard to remove, and that virtue and vice pass down the generations.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Changed over time. The Trew Law (1598) says the king is above the law and is bound to it only by good will. By 1609 he said a king in a settled kingdom is bound by the fundamental laws through his coronation oath and becomes a tyrant if he leaves them, though only God can judge him.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Rejected the 'Aristocratick and limited gouernment' of Venice as no free monarchy and called monarchy the best form, though he described England as a king in Parliament.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Same 1609 position: apostates from his church should be struck hardest by the law. He applied it to conversion to Catholicism, not to leaving religion in general.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: No stated position on the general principle; his union of the English and Scottish crowns is something nearby.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Told his son to honour the nobility as 'Peeres and Fathers of your land' and to serve himself with men of the noblest blood.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Called Highlanders and islanders 'barbarous' and ordered colonies among them to 'reforme and ciuilize' them; in 1609 described the Irish as barbarous and urged plantation there.

elective-rulers.rationale: Contrasted 'free monarchies' with 'electiue kings' and the Doge of Venice, and held that succession is by birth and not by election.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Held that a tyrant, idolater or breaker of oaths must still be obeyed without resistance, only prayed for and fled, and that Parliament and people have no right to unmake him.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Said Parliament is 'the Kings great Councell', that no Parliament law has force without his sceptre, and that the king made the laws, not the laws the king.

native-born-offices.rationale: Told his son never to put a foreigner in any principal office of state and to choose natives of each country as chief counsellors there. He limited this to principal offices.

filial-duty.rationale: Told his son to honour his parents, his mother above all, and those in the place of parents, as God's law commands.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Inferred: held that members of Parliament are 'sworne Councellours' of the king and that grievances are for the king, not for binding instructions from constituents.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Mixed: asked Parliament for supply in 1609 and called the amount a matter of 'your loues', but also said subjects' goods are due to him and that Parliament must not dispute his power.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Told his son not to supply or trust other princes' rebels and to count rebellion against any prince a crime against himself.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Held that subjects must obey the king as God's lieutenant in everything except what is directly against God.

non-intervention.rationale: Points both ways: denied the Pope any right to meddle between a king and his subjects (1608), but told his son to succour lawful princes in trouble and in 1609 sent troops to Cleves.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Points both ways: blamed the Gunpowder Plot on papal doctrine and Jesuits and said papists were growing proud in 1609, but also said many Catholics were loyal and should not be blamed.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Treated marriage as ordained by God and tied to the legal succession of legitimate children, and told his son to keep his marriage vow.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Said a king need not give an account of his actions to his people, only to declare his heart, and that subjects must not dispute his power; he opened the royal accounts to Parliament in 1609 as a favour 'Kings doe seldome bestow'.

religious-nation.rationale: Said in 1603 that Catholics who differ in religion 'cannot bee but halfe my Subiects'; he also said loyal Catholics were not to be persecuted for conscience.

religion-illusion.rationale: Held that true religion grounded on Scripture is the basis of all government and that blessing on a throne depends on it.

majority-settlement.rationale: Planned and urged colonies of lowland ('inland') subjects among Highlanders and islanders, and in 1609 spoke of the Plantation of Ulster as his policy against the rebels there.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Listed sodomy among the horrible crimes a king is bound in conscience never to forgive. Historians dispute his own relationships with male favourites; the statement is about his stated view of the law.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Told his son to punish Puritan leaders who incite rebellion and to forbid church meetings without leave; but he also invited grievances in Parliament and said he never blamed those who raised them properly.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Called witchcraft 'the highest poynt of Idolatrie' punishable by death (1597), and wanted recusants presented under the law, but said in 1609 that God never plants his church by violence and bloodshed.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Said kings sit on God's throne, are God's lieutenants, and that the power to make a king is God's alone: 'he that hath the only power to make him, hath the onely power to vnmake him'.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Told his son how to wage war and kept a standing army in Ireland and garrisons, saying in 1609 he dared not let it be reduced.

dynastic-succession.rationale: Held that the crown passes by birth to the nearest heir, 'heritable ouer-lord', and urged his son to leave all his kingdoms to his eldest son.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Asked in 1607 for law to be cleared and certain, preferring 'a certaine Law with some spots' to arbitrary law, and said in 1609 a king who stops ruling by his laws becomes a tyrant; he also reserved the right to mitigate or suspend laws.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Called a 'leaprouse conscience' the mother of atheism and told his son to maintain the church and schools in purity.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Inferred: made strict execution of the laws the king's chief duty and told him to punish offenders severely before showing mercy.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: At Hampton Court in 1604 he persuaded the bishops that only ministers should baptise, ending baptism by women; he did not discuss women's ordination.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Told his son: 'command her as her Lord ... It is your office to command, and hers to obey'.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Gave the case of an honest man who kills one of several brigands in self-defence and asked whether he should lose his head: 'Surely no'.

second-chamber.rationale: Described Parliament as an Upper House of nobles and bishops and a Lower House of knights and burgesses and wanted the three estates re-established in Scotland.

person-over-state.rationale: Mixed: said the king is ordained for the people and not the people for him, but also said the head may cut off rotten members for the body's good.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Said the king must procure 'the weale of both soules and bodies' of those in his charge.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Promised in 1603 never to give the first occasion of a breach of peace, but said wars on just quarrels are lawful, including to avenge foreign injuries and the honour of the kingdom.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Wrote that 'a Prince can neuer without secrecie doe great things'.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Told his son to root out the nobles' private feuds and to enforce his laws against guns and pistols; revenge by private persons is 'usurping your office, to whom the sword belongeth'.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Told his son to be severe in martial discipline and to suppress mutinies, which he called very dangerous in war.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Called his Protestant faith 'the onely trew forme of Gods worship' and Catholic doctrine 'mysterie of iniquitie'.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Said in 1603 that his religion alone was 'the trew Religion, which by me is professed, and by the Law is established', and treated Puritans and Catholics as sects outside it.

premarital-sex.rationale: Told his son that fornication is a grave sin and that he should come to marriage clean; in the same passage he said a wife should be a pure virgin.

women-suffrage.rationale: Told his son never to let his wife meddle in government, and described the accession of a woman as a 'double curse' on Scotland.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Wrote that the whole Scripture is 'dyted by Gods Spirit' and that 'no booke nor Law is perfect nor free from corruption, except onely the booke and Law of God'.

national-church-status.rationale: Defended the Church of England as the one 'by Law established' and later tried to bring the Scottish Kirk 'so neir as can be' to it, with bishops.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: Did the opposite: ordered settlers planted among Highlanders and islanders and pushed the Ulster plantation.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Said even a just prince takes no subject's life 'without a cleare law', and in Daemonologie told judges to beware convicting the innocent.

self-ownership.rationale: Held that the king has 'power ouer the life and death of euery one' of his subjects, and that kings may dispose of subjects' bodies and goods.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Said in 1616 that municipal law that does not depend on God's law is 'vniust and vnlawful'; he also held that subjects must still not resist the king's commands, only refuse what is directly against God.

notes: Changes of view: the Trew Law (1598) places the king above the law, bound only by good will; by 1609-10 he said a king in a settled kingdom is bound by its fundamental laws through his oath, while still accountable to God alone, and the later position is used. Witchcraft: Daemonologie (1597) demands death; later accounts of a more sceptical James are not used here. Basilikon Doron was written for his son and is advice, not law; statements drawn from it are marked accordingly. Opened but not usable for any statement: A Counterblaste to Tobacco beyond its opening pages (its tobacco-specific argument matches no statement except a low-confidence drug answer); the Wikipedia Treaty of London (1604) article (background only). The King James Bible and the later parts of the Oath of Allegiance apology and the Premonition were not read in full. The 'no bishop, no king' remark at Hampton Court is reported by Barlow, a secondhand source not opened here; the point is taken from Basilikon Doron instead.
